The closing of Life Esidimeni psychiatric hospitals

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We find out what has happened to the 2000 psychiatric patients after the government closed its contract with Life Esidimeni

Summary:
2000 Vulnerable psychiatric patients have been moved to understaffed and ill-equipped NGO's across gauteng after the government cancelled its contract with Esidimeni life hospital.

40 of the 2000 were moved to a small in NGO in Lanseria where the owner Patricia, who may need to remain anonymous, was promised by the government that she would be provided the funding to care for them. That was two months ago, still they have no beds, no clothing, no extra care givers and Patricia has now had to take money from her own pocket to care for these people. They are sleeping on the floor at the moment.
Barbra's uncle is one of these 40 people, he is 50 years old and suffers from dementia.

Gaba's 30 year old daughter Dorothy was moved without her consent. All loved ones where promised that they would be able to assess the NGO before their family members were moved, this did not happen. Dorothy was moved to Takalani in Soweto. When she was at life she was to be able to communicate when she needed needed to go to the toilet or how she was feeling, now she does not talk at all. She is in nappies, as the nurses say she can't communicate when she needs to the toilet. At Takalani there is 1 caregiver for every 14 patients. They start waking the patients up at 2:30am to shower, as the one caregiver has to wash and dress all 14 patients. Dorothy also has an injury on her head and hand that no-one can explain and no report of an accident has been explained to her mother.

3rd case study - I am looking for a family member who has someone at Hammenskraal where there are 40 patients to one long drop

Specialists:
Lawyer from section 27 who was fighting the protocol of the shutdown, he has evidence that patients being medicated for hyposexuality and hypoaggresison were moved to a children's unit at takalani
Dr Talatala - SASOP

Press Release:


Mental Healthcare Contract Terminated
In June, the Gauteng Health Department terminated its contract with Life Esidimeni, a company caring for state and private patients with serious psychiatric disorders. This shock move saw hundreds of patients placed in the care of critically under-equipped NGOs and others back into the care of relatives. Civil society groups and family members have raised serious concerns, saying patients were relocated with minimal consultation. Carte Blanche asks: is this a viable plan or is government shirking its responsibilities?


Script:


Time code Description / Visual
00: 00 Norma sitting with her dog outside reading a book. Norma: She was a perfect little child very good, very clever at school never naughty.
00:10 Devi interview with Norma about Julia her daughter. Devi How long has Julia been in mental health for?
Norma: Somewhere between 25 – 30 years since she was 16.
Devi: what was Julia diagnosed with?
Norma: chronic Treatment resistance paranoia skisophrinia People with her type of condition are not suitable to live in normal environment you are setting them up to fail. They cain’t marry they cain’t hold down a job they cain’t have children they cain’t manage their finances so from that point of view I realized I had to accept that a care center was the best environment for her for her. They managed to get her on to a dosage of which she could manage where she wasn’t paranoid when she was coming home she could was doing dishes and make coffee for me so that was her maintain dosage she took it twice a day.

00:59 Christina explaining about her sister and how she died. Christine: my sister name was Virginia, when my mom passed away she which was in the early 1992 she basically raised us there is 5 of us, she was the eldest. We basically did everything together. In 2014 she disappeared from home for about 2 and half days and nobody knew where she was so obviously we put out a search party put out that she is missing and something is wrong. Immediately came to live with me and I took her to the Dr. to find out what was wrong. The Doctor said to us “from here I recommend that she doesn’t come home with us but go to a facility. And the Dr. said to us that the best facility for us would be Life Esidimeni,
01:46 – Devi Link to camera Devi: for almost 40 years the department of health had a private partnership with Life Esidimeni to take care of mentally ill patients then in 2015 the Department announced they are cancelling the contract. Alternate arrangements will be made for the patience’s and this is where our story begins.
00:29 – 02:39 Devi V/O V/O: in 2015 this contract with Life Esidimeni cost the Gauteng Department of Health 20 million Rands. This need to save costs together with the mental health policy which states that mentally ill patiences should be reintergrated back into the community with the 2 driving forces the termination of this contract for better or for worse the contract is now over and the patience have been moved. But were the NGO’s, the patients, the Families prepared for this massive relocation.
02:39 – 03:03 Interview with Dr. DR: I have worked at Randfontein working in a ward that actually decided whether a patient goes home or stays longer at Randfontein or goes to an NGO or Life Esidimeni. The best prize is to send the patient home, the 2nd prize is to send the patient to an NGO the worst thing that we did was to send them to Life Esidimeni. Those were the patients that were untreatable. In medical terms we call that Refractory illness.
03:02 – 03:09 Devi: Julia was moved from Life Esidimeni to an NGO in Soweto without Norma being informed.
03:09- 03:28 Devi and Norma interview Devi: how did you managed to find out that she was moved to Siyabathanda?
Norma: I phoned one day to ask what was going on with Julia’s placement they told me that she had been moved to Siyabathanda you start to panic you don’t know where your child is and if she is happy or how she is feeling its an awful experience.
03:28 - 03:37 D V/O: Siyathemba is an NGO that was set up in braamfischer Soweto solely for the purpose of housing 14 women from Life Esidimeni.
03:38 – 03:52 Devi: you phoned up Siyabanthanda?
Norma: and well I said I would like to come out and see her. She brought Julia to me to meet her, at South Gate and on the African kombi. We went back to check the NGO
03:52 – 04:24 Hidden Camera of Siyabathanda environment. Devi: After being denied access to the NGO we took in a hidden camera, we were shocked to find that these 14 chroniclly ill women were living in a small 2 bedroom house. They we sharing 2 bathrooms and they was no way for them to do any sort of recreational activity whixch is essential for mentally ill patients. Cassey Chambers from the South African Depression and Anxiety Group has been helping the families, patients and NGO’s during this relocation.
04:24 – 04:47 Caseey chambers Cassey: many of these NGO from the informational that we getting and speaking to them were started for this patience’s to be discharged to. So they are new or setting up, for the first time dealing with severely mentally ill patience’s they properly trained or built capacity and that’s what we are trying to help them now is that we are trying to have the proper programs ion place.
04:47 – 05:00 Conditions of Siyabathanda Devi V/O: like so many of thr NGO’s the owner of Siyabathanda has been battling to get the necessary medication from the local clincs as they were not prepared for the influx of patients from Life Esidimeni and their specialized needs.
05:00 – 06:23 Devi speaks to Norma about Julia’s health and not doing well. And the situation with medication with Norma. Devi: when did you find out that Julia wasn’t doing well?
Norma: I phone a month or so ago to bring her out for LOA.
Devi: LOA – Leave of Absence,
Norma: yeah leave of absence, Thembi said that “oh she was so worried now because Julia wasn’t well she is in hospital” well said “why would she be ill and in hospital” and I didn’t get full details because it had something to do with not having the medication and they took her to the clinic and the clinic didn’t have medication and I assumed that between all of them who are not properly trained to look after them and the patients that they hadn’t given her the medication.
Devi: she is in hospital as we speak?
Norma: As we speak,
Devi which hospital?
Norma: Baragwaneth
Devi: and the reason? She had a relapse?
Norma: a complete total breakdown, years of work that the doctors have put in to stabilize her and obviously the doctor feels that its not just an odd day or so that they didn’t give medication its probably over the 2 months or so. When I go to see her now at Baragwaneth hospital its an ordeal to see her,
- 06:23 Footage of Julia in hospital. Norma: she s slightly better than yesterday.
06:24 – 06:28 Devi: We went to MEC of Health for answers.
06:28 – 07:30 Devi speaks to MEC about the medication situations. The promises and issues that the NGO are facing and not being ready to host the patience. Devi: the patience relapses completely because there is no medication and these are the gaps that we are finding especially with a lot of the new NGO specifically.

Devi: why did you send these patience to places that they were not ready?
MEC: you go an asses the facilities and people say that we are doing this where can we meet the criteria.
Devi: not good enough MEC people lie. What I’m saying is maybe it would’ve been better if we kept the patients where they were for a little but longer while these NGO set up shop
MEC: the mistake in this particular incident that we are referring to the NGO over stated their capacity. whoever that decided that patience have been placed in places that are not equipped I will take responsibility for those people because we have to look after the interest of the patience’s

07:44 – 08:20 Christina situation with her sister being moved to an NGO without her knowledge. Ethel called her telling her she is a director and the request that they had to move her 2 weeks prior and she passed away. Christine: On Thursday the 25 of August, I received a call from a lady called Ethel. She told me she was a director of Precious Angle Care home. And she was telling me that Cullinan had requested that my sister be moved to her for special treatment stimulation treatment and she had been moved two weeks prior to that day that she was called me on the 25th and she was telling me8that my sister was no more she had passed away.
08:21 – 08:47 Christians sister death certificate and what she died from. The mix up of the dates and Ethel refusing to give the address to the facility. V/O: Christine was told by the Ethel the owner of Precious Special care that her sister had passed away on the 17th of august but when she got the paramedics report it stated that her sister had died on the 15th of August.
Christine: We spoke to Ethel if she could give us the address of Precious NGO she basically didn’t want to give it to us.
08:47 – 09:05 V/O

Christina on the quest to find her sisters body. The pain that she went through V/O: after being denied access to the NGO where her sister had passed away, Christine began the search to find her sisters body she was told it was at a mortuary in Archriville but when she arrived it was clearly not there. Eventually she located her sister in a mortuary in Soshengove
09:05 – 09:14 Christine: we did see her; we did see her and she looked peaceful yeah.
09:14 -09:24 Devi explaining that Christina found other bodies that were from the Ngo Devi: Christine then discovered that there were 6 other bodies there all from precious angel care they had arrived within the past two months.
08:47 – 10:25 Devi speaking to MEC about the bodies that were found at the mortuary from Precious Angel Care.
Devi and MEC discussing the visitation of the NGO Devi: apparently there were 6 bodies that came specifically over a period of time and this place was opened in June from Precious Angel Care, now we need to flag that and get to the bottom of that
MEC: what is the name of that place?
Devi: Precious angle care
MEC: okay let me investigate that
Devi: she has opened a case at the police and she has a case number
MEC: that’s good that she opened the case I will make sure there is proper investigation
Devi: but who from the department of health goes and visits these NGO?
MEC: the team is visiting them once a week and once a week I sit with them to get a report to see what’s going on hence we’ve been able to where there is no medication we intervene and but where there are still problems I continue to be con8cerned…
Devi: you must be shocked then when I’m telling about places like Siyabathanda, because if the department went to go visit these places every single week this would’ve been flagged a long time ago
MEC: no I will attend to them and I just want to apologies to those families and the patience concerned we will get to the bottom of this matter.

10:25 – 10:51 Christina explaining what her sister means to her and that she could’ve taken care of her by herself Christine: my sister my mean nothing to somebody else but she is my sister to me she means the world, and they had no right to do that and if they didn’t want to take care of her they should’ve told me to take care of her I would’ve rather struggled at home but to actually. If you were to see this house that she died

metadata.Summary: 2000 Vulnerable psychiatric patients have been moved to understaffed and ill-equipped NGO's across gauteng after the government cancelled its contract with Esidimeni life hospital. 40 of the 2000 were moved to a small in NGO in Lanseria where the owner Patricia, who may need to remain anonymous, was promised by the government that she would be provided the funding to care for them. That was two months ago, still they have no beds, no clothing, no extra care givers and Patricia has now had to take money from her own pocket to care for these people. They are sleeping on the floor at the moment. Barbra's uncle is one of these 40 people, he is 50 years old and suffers from dementia. Gaba's 30 year old daughter Dorothy was moved without her consent. All loved ones where promised that they would be able to assess the NGO before their family members were moved, this did not happen. Dorothy was moved to Takalani in Soweto. When she was at life she was to be able to communicate when she needed needed to go to the toilet or how she was feeling, now she does not talk at all. She is in nappies, as the nurses say she can't communicate when she needs to the toilet. At Takalani there is 1 caregiver for every 14 patients. They start waking the patients up at 2:30am to shower, as the one caregiver has to wash and dress all 14 patients. Dorothy also has an injury on her head and hand that no-one can explain and no report of an accident has been explained to her mother. 3rd case study - I am looking for a family member who has someone at Hammenskraal where there are 40 patients to one long drop Specialists: Lawyer from section 27 who was fighting the protocol of the shutdown, he has evidence that patients being medicated for hyposexuality and hypoaggresison were moved to a children's unit at takalani Dr Talatala - SASOP Health MEC for gauteng?
metadata.Expert: Mr. DR. Talatala Ms. Cassie Chambers
